title: Swiatek fends off Bejlek to reach Toronto third round
description: Former world number one Iga Swiatek survived some nervy moments to launch her US Open build-up with a 6-0, 6-3 victory over Sara Bejlek in her second-round opener at the Toronto WTA 1000 on Tuesday.World number one Aryna Sabalenka was due to open her campaign on Tuesday night with a second-round clash against Japanese qualifier Moyuka Uchijima.
fullText:
Former world number one Iga Swiatek survived some nervy moments to launch her US Open build-up with a 6-0, 6-3 victory over Sara Bejlek in her second-round opener at the Toronto WTA 1000 on Tuesday.

In her first match since her Wimbledon title defense ended with a third-round exit, Poland's Swiatek was rolling through the first nine games, appearing in total control with a double-break for a 3-0 lead in the second.

But her Czech opponent dug in, using off-speed balls and some well-judged volleys to disrupt Swiatek's rhythm, winning two straight games before Swiatek pulled off a great escape -- fending off nine break points in a 22-minute sixth game to hold serve for a 4-2 lead.

"It was quite a weird game I've got to say," Swiatek gold Tennis Channel. "Not easy to finish it. There was much more running, much more different change of rhythm and different solutions that we used during that game.

"I felt like we both were kind of changing the rhythm and the pace all the time, so sometimes it was hard to adjust to it.

"I'm happy that I stayed in the game and stayed solid because I felt at the end it got pretty physical."

Swiatek has slipped from third in the world at this time last year to her current eighth.

Her Wimbledon disappointment came just four weeks after the four-time French Open champion bowed out in the last 16 at Roland Garros.

In fact, Swiatek has yet to reach a Tour-level final this season and is hoping a late surge over the North American hard court campaign capped by the US Open will prevent her from finishing the calendar year without a title for the first time since 2020 -- the year she won the first of her six Grand Slam titles at Roland Garros.

She took some of the extra time after Wimbledon to work on technical aspects of her game, saying she's been working on her rhythm and not rushing on the court.

"I feel like for sure in practices I already have these new habits in me. Sometimes during the match you've just got to focus even more to not let these old patterns come back."

World number one Aryna Sabalenka was due to open her campaign on Tuesday night with a second-round clash against Japanese qualifier Moyuka Uchijima.

Sabalenka is also looking to bounce back on the hard courts of North America after falling in the quarter-finals at Roland Garros and in the round of 16 at Wimbledon.

The Belarusian star has dominated on the surface this year, winning 23 of her 24 matches on hard courts -- the lone defeat her loss to Elena Rybakina in the Australian Open final.

In other early matches, ninth-seeded Ukrainian Elina Svitolina rallied from a set and a break down to beat Spain's Jessica Bouzas Maneiro 6-7 (5/7), 7-6 (7/4), 6-4.

Ukraine's French Open finalist Marta Kostyuk was also in action, taking on Canadian wild card Katherine Sebov.

title: Angels DFA former All-Star, World Series MVP Jorge Soler
description: Soler hit three home runs en route to winning World Series MVP with the Braves in 2021 and has been an All-Star since.
fullText:
The Los Angeles Angels have designated Jorge Soler for assignment, according to multiple reports, ending his time with the club.

The transaction removes Soler from their 40-man roster, and they now have seven days to either release him, trade him or place him on waivers. The move comes a day after MLB's trade deadline.

Soler, 34, is a former All-Star who won World Series MVP with the Atlanta Braves in 2021. Soler hit three home runs in the series that helped propel the Braves past the Houston Astros in six games. He played two seasons with the Miami Marlins after that World Series and was named an All-Star in 2023.

Soler spent the 2024 season split between the Braves and San Francisco Giants before joining the Angeles in 2024 via trade from the Braves. He's playing on the third year of a three-year, $42 million contract that he signed to join the Giants in 2024.

Soler has regressed at the plate this season with a slash line of .203/.291/.273 in 86 games. He's remained productive despite his diminished hitting with 12 home runs and 49 RBI. A former full-time outfielder, Soler has played primarily this season at designated hitter. The Angels are in last place in the AL West at 43-69.

Soler's 215 career home runs and postseason experience could make him attractive to a contending team seeking to add depth. Whether any team thinks it's worth taking on the remainder of his salary rather than wait for him to clear waivers or be released is another story.

title: Ireland's McFerran out of World Cup through injury
description: Distinguished Ireland goalkeeper Ayeisha McFerran is ruled out of the forthcoming Hockey World Cup through injury.
fullText:
Ireland's women must plan for the forthcoming World Cup without distinguished goalkeeper Ayeisha McFerran, who has been ruled out of the tournament through injury.

McFerran's many achievements in the game included being named Goalkeeper of the Tournament at the 2018 World Cup, at which Ireland were silver medallists.

Head coach Gareth Grundie has announced a 20-player squad to travel to Wavre, Belgium.

In McFerran's absence, Lizzy Murphy and Holly Micklem are named, offering them their first chance to potentially represent Ireland in goal on one of hockey's biggest stages.

The side will be making their third successive appearance at at a World Cup, having beaten Japan in a shootout in the bronze medal match in Santiago to ensure qualification for the 2026 edition.

Ireland, who are ranked 12th in the world, have been drawn in Pool C of the competition, and will face Spain in their opening match on 16 August, before playing New Zealand two days later and Belgium on 20 August.

A top-two finish in the pool would allow Ireland to progress to Pool E for a shot at a place in the semi-finals, while a third or fourth place finish would send them to Pool H where they will begin their final classification matches.

Meanwhile, Ireland men's coach Mark Tumilty has also announced a 20-strong squad as the side prepare to make their first appearance in the competition since 2018.

Tumilty has named an unchanged squad from that which secured qualification in Santiago in March courtesy of a comprehensive semi-final win over Wales, before coming from behind to beat France in the final.

Ireland's men are 10th in the world rankings and have been drawn in Pool C of the competition, taking on Australia in their opener on Sunday, 16 August, before facing South Africa and Spain on 18 and 20 August respectively.

As with the women, a top-two place would put the team into Pool E for a semi-final chance, while they would enter Pool H for classification fixtures if they come third or fourth.

title: Cape Verde coach Bubista resigns as Ivory Coast reappoint Renard
description: Head coach Bubista leaves Cape Verde after reaching the last 32 at the World Cup while Ivory Coast reappoint two-time Afcon winner Herve Renard.
fullText:
Bubista has resigned from his post as Cape Verde head coach to join Moroccan club RS Berkane while Ivory Coast have hired Herve Renard for a second spell in charge.

Bubista guided the island nation to the last 32 of the World Cup last month, where the Blue Sharks were beaten 3-2 by eventual runners-up Argentina after extra time.

The 56-year-old also reached the quarter-finals of the 2023 Africa Cup of Nations with Cape Verde, having taken charge in January 2020.

He has signed a two-year deal with RS Berkane, who finished second in the Moroccan top flight last season, and replaces Moin Chaabani, who has been appointed as Tunisia's new head coach.

Renard has won the Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) twice as a coach including with Ivory Coast in 2015. He previously led Zambia to a fairy tale title in 2012.

The Ivorians lost 2-1 to Norway in the last 32 at the World Cup and decided not to renew Emerse Fae's deal when it expired at the end of last month.

The former Nantes and Reading midfielder took over the reins midway through the 2023 Afcon - after the Elephants had failed in a bid to reappoint Renard - and the tournament hosts were crowned champions following a remarkable run through the knockout stage.

Renard has had stints with Morocco, Saudi Arabia (twice) and France's women since leaving Ivory Coast in May 2015, and was in the dugout for Tunisia for two games at this year's World Cup.

The length of the 57-year-old's contract has not been disclosed and the Frenchman is expected in Abidjan "in the coming days" to take up his official duties.

Bubista's sustained success with Cape Verde has raised his profile across the continent.

And while RS Berkane, from the north-east of Morocco, are not traditionally seen as one of the kingdom's big clubs they have enjoyed success in recent years.

They claimed their first domestic league title in 2024-25 and are three-time winners of the Caf Confederation Cup, Africa's second tier continental club competition.

Berkane caused controversy in 2024 by wearing a shirt in the Confederation Cup which featured a map of Morocco including the disputed territory of Western Sahara.

Cape Verde qualified for the World Cup for the first time ahead of Cameroon and the debutants proved to be the underdog story of this year's finals.

Cape Verde's football federation thanked Bubista for his "dedication, professionalism, and contribution to the development of the national team's sporting project" before wishing him "much success" in his future endeavours.

Bubista becomes the latest coach to leave one of the 10 African sides which appeared at the World Cup.

Vladimir Petkovic parted company with Algeria, who exited against Switzerland in the last 32, by mutual consent on Monday.

The 62-year-old Bosnian, who was appointed in February 2024, had extended his contract with the Desert Foxes until 2028 earlier this year.

Meanwhile, Hugo Broos stepped down as South Africa boss when his contract expired at the end of July, with the 74-year-old deciding to retire from management.

Senegal sacked Pape Thiaw in the wake of their dramatic last-32 exit against Belgium, with the country's football federation saying it had made the decision "in the best interests of Senegalese football".

The Teranga Lions have been linked with former France and Arsenal midfielder Patrick Vieira as a possible replacement.

Elsewhere, Tunisia appointed Chaabani on a four-year deal last month.

The 45-year-old replaced Renard, who himself took over the Carthage Eagles one game into their Group F campaign when Sabri Lamouchi was removed after a 5-1 defeat by Sweden.

Internal discussions are continuing at the Ghana Football Association after Carlos Queiroz led the Black Stars to the last 32, where the West Africans lost 1-0 to Colombia.

Queiroz appeared to announce his own departure on social media shortly after that defeat.

title: Nuclear Safety Authority supports spent nuclear fuel final disposal facility
description: On 4 August 2026, the Radiation and Nuclear Safety Authority issued a statement to the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment on Posiva Oy’s application for a licence to operate a spent nuclear fuel encapsulation and final disposal facility. According to STUK, the safety requirements required for granting the operating licence are met. This is the first time in the world that the geological final disposal facility for spent nuclear fuel has progressed to the operating licence phase.
fullText:
On 4 August 2026, the Radiation and Nuclear Safety Authority issued a statement to the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment on Posiva Oy’s application for a licence to operate a spent nuclear fuel encapsulation and final disposal facility. According to STUK, the safety requirements required for granting the operating licence are met. This is the first time in the world that the geological final disposal facility for spent nuclear fuel has progressed to the operating licence phase.

In its statement, the Radiation and Nuclear Safety Authority (STUK) states that the encapsulation and final disposal facility for spent nuclear fuel Posiva built in Olkiluoto, Eurajoki meets the safety requirements set for it in the Nuclear Energy Act and Decree. Therefore, there is no obstacle to granting the facility an operating licence with regard to radiation and nuclear safety.

"This is a significant step in the final disposal of spent nuclear fuel that has been prepared for more than 40 years. STUK has been assessing and overseeing the safety of final disposal over several decades. Based on the overall assessment we have now made, we can conclude that the safety requirements for granting the operating permit are met," says Petteri Tiippana, STUK’s Director General.

The Government decides on whether to grant the operating licence for the final disposal facility based on preparatory work by the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment. STUK’s favourable statement is a prerequisite for granting the operating licence. Even if the Government was to grant the operating licence, final disposal cannot yet be started. Before commencing operations, STUK shall confirm in a separate decision that the encapsulation and final disposal facility meets all safety requirements set for the start of operation.

In the final disposal solution selected by Posiva, the high-level spent nuclear fuel is enclosed in final disposal canisters in an above-ground encapsulation plant. The canisters will then be permanently placed in a final disposal facility built in the bedrock at a depth of 400–450 metres. The spent nuclear fuel is thus isolated from people and the living environment by several complementary release barriers. These include the final disposal canister made of iron and copper, the surrounding bentonite clay and the bedrock itself.

"The safety of final disposal is not dependent on a single structure or material. The safety is based on a combination of a canister, bentonite clay and bedrock, which prevents and slows down the release and migration of radioactive substances into the environment," says Jaakko Leino, Director of Nuclear Waste and Regulation.

Posiva is currently applying for an operating licence until the end of 2070. STUK will also monitor Posiva’s operations during the facility’s operation pursuant to the Nuclear Energy Act.

The safety assessment also covers long-term safety

In the safety assessment, STUK has examined both the safety of the encapsulation and final disposal facility during the operation phase and the long-term safety of the final disposal. The long-term safety assessment examines the development of the final disposal system and its environment over very long periods of time and how the release and transmission of radioactive substances into the environment is prevented and slowed down. In addition, STUK has assessed the readiness of Posiva’s organisation to start operation of the encapsulation and final disposal facility.

STUK’s statement is based on a long and thorough safety assessment. "Demonstrating safety has been the starting point for the assessment throughout. We have reviewed a great amount of technical data and safety analyses and monitored Posiva’s operations in many ways," says Antti Tynkkynen, Project Manager for the Posiva regulatory control project. Since 2000, STUK and its external experts have contributed a total of more than 250 man-years to project supervision and safety licence assessment.

Safety assessment and development continues

STUK proposes conditions for the operating licence to ensure the continuation of safety assessment and development also during the facility's operation.

STUK proposes that Posiva must carry out the first periodic safety assessment within ten years of granting the operating licence. At the same time, Posiva must update the long-term safety justification to correspond to the final disposal system to be deployed. In addition, Posiva must provide STUK with detailed plans for the final disposal facility for low- and intermediate-level waste and a safety justification for long-term safety based on them before the construction of the final disposal facility in question begins.

"As the operation phase begins, we will gain the first experience of how the plans, methodological tests and systems of the world’s first geological final disposal facility for spent nuclear fuel work in practice. These experiences must be used to learn and further develop the operations and safety, as necessary," Tynkkynen says.

Read more about this topic on the Posiva Final Disposal Facility page.

The Danube River's water is dropping so low that World War II ships are emerging
description: Water levels on the Danube River, the second longest in Europe, have dropped so low because of drought that the hulks of dozens of World War II German battleships are emerging into view.  The Danube’s...
fullText:
PRAHOVO, Serbia (AP) — Water levels on the Danube River, the second longest in Europe, have dropped so low because of drought that the hulks of dozens of World War II German battleships are emerging into view.

They are a curious distraction from the summer heat crisis. The Danube's record low water levels also have forced power plants to the brink of shutting down, and governments across Central and Eastern Europe are taking steps to conserve electricity.

In the middle of the river separating Serbia and Romania near the Serbian port of Prahovo, a rusty hull is now visible along with a broken mast where the Nazi flag used to fly.

The ships, some still laden with weapons, belonged to Nazi Germany's Black Sea fleet that the Germans deliberately sank as they retreated from Romania and as Soviet forces advanced deeper into Europe near the end of the war.

Historians say up to 200 German warships were scuttled in September 1944 near Prahovo in the Danube gorge as they came under Soviet fire. The idea behind the deliberate sinking was to slow down the Soviet advance in the Balkans. But Nazi Germany surrendered months later, in May 1945.

The sight of the old warships is a reminder that the Serbian government, with European Union financial support, has long been trying to do something about them. Some were removed from the river by Communist Yugoslav authorities, but most have remained because of the explosives they carried.

Now, however, authorities are trying to keep traffic flowing on the Danube, which flows through 10 nations, as the dropping water levels create dangerous conditions. Experts have linked the unusually hot weather to global warming and other factors.

Krsta Brandic, a Prahovo resident, said the low water levels have almost stopped ship traffic: "As you can see, the (big) ships can't pass anymore."

The creators of Untitled Goose Game return with an online, open-world adventure that delivers slapstick silliness and bucolic majesty in nearly equal measure

Radiant sunsets glinting on lapping waves; bushland valleys that beckon with secrets; modernist buildings sat atop craggy ridges: Big Walk’s setting is as arresting as it is beguiling – a kind of architectural fever dream transplanted to a handsome Australian wilderness – but it is the images created by players that lodge deepest in the mind. Here’s one that has stuck with me: in the black of night, cicadas kicking up an almighty din, I had lost my partner. Panic. Despair. Fear. Then, there in the far distance, I saw him signalling in my direction. He was relentlessly spamming a gigantic, ball-shaped lamp on and off, the ground around him flicking from inky dark to warm pastel pink and back again, like a single Christmas light blinking from afar.

This kind of encounter is common in Big Walk, the brilliant and whimsical new online co-op puzzler from House House, the Melbourne-based studio behind the 2019 viral hit, Untitled Goose Game. Rather than playing as a honking, mischief-making goose as you do in that game, you are a bug-eyed, gangly limbed kind of bird person (think Pingu as drawn by Mondrian) for whom getting separated from your mates is all part of the fun. That’s somewhat because this rugged terrain is dense with vegetation and cliffs to fall down, and also because the game makes ingenious use of proximity and direction-based voice audio. Step out of earshot of your party and you will find it difficult to call for one another (unless, of course, you’ve picked up a Fisher-Price-like walkie-talkie).

So you and up to 12 players step out into this somewhat eerily photorealistic open world to uncover its mysteries. Quickly, you come across challenges which veer from the straightforward to the brain-scrambling: shoot the aforementioned ball-shaped lamp into a hoop; arrange wooden pegs decorated with odd, nature-themed symbols into some kind of shape. For each successfully completed task, you win what looks like a large red peanut. Get enough of these red peanuts and you score a key which in turn unlocks some important piece of infrastructure: for example, a slow-moving, toy-like train whose parping horns are a joy to obnoxiously blare across the otherwise bucolic landscape.

This structure naturally sustains its own rhythm: moments of intense cooperative concentration followed by longer stretches of ambulatory downtime. Such is the layout of this world, you end up doing a lot of backtracking. This is when a little of the game’s quirky lustre wears off since the actual walking is the least interesting part of Big Walk (and you’re also liable to get stuck on bits of rock). Frustration builds as you traipse through the same patch of scrub for the umpteenth time.

Still, Big Walk’s less action-packed moments can be gratifying in their own way: I never tired of watching the twinkling night sky segue with impossible speed into the warm, orange glow of a new day, or stopping to enjoy the sounds of a softly gurgling creak.

The beauty of Big Walk lies in how it tasks you with working together, conversing verbally and physically, to access its most enchanting sights. It stands out in an era when so much of online communication, be that in video games or on social media, has been distorted by a kind of attention-holding logic – for instance, the serotonin-releasing kerching of notifications or the relentless rewards of levelling up. Yet Big Walk eschews these pernicious aspects of digital life for a gentler, less overbearing experience that seems expressly designed to foster enriching connections and childlike playfulness.

Here’s another moment that has stuck with me: wiping away tears of laughter after my brother and I clumsily dropped one of those essential red peanuts to the bottom of the devilishly constructed, practically “masocore” 100ft shaft that we had painstakingly platformed our way out of. We nattered about it until we found the next thing that piqued our interest: wobbly rave tunes blaring from deep inside the belly of a mountain. I shan’t say any more: you and your pals will want to discover these delights for yourselves.

title: Fifa private money plan had to be scrapped - Wenger
description: Fifa's chief of global football development Arsene Wenger says the decision to scrap the plan to have private investment in Fifa competitions was "absolutely necessary".
fullText:
Fifa's chief of global football development Arsene Wenger says scrapping the plan to have private investment in Fifa competitions was "absolutely necessary and beyond question".

Fifa president Gianni Infantino planned to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, with external investors able to buy stakes.

Infantino had offered Fifa's 211 member associations $40m (£30m) each if they backed the proposal.

But after days of criticism - including Uefa's 55 nations threatening to boycott all Fifa tournaments - Infantino was forced to withdraw the plan.

Wenger has been in a role which encompasses data analysis of the game, Fifa's online training and youth competitions since 2019.

The former Arsenal boss previously supported Infantino's proposal to play the men's World Cup every two years.

A week after Infantino's investment plan was first released, the Frenchman issued a statement through Fifa in which he demanded "transparency and integrity" from world football's governing body.

"The recent events at Fifa deserve some clarity from my side," Wenger's statement read.

"I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports.

"The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent Fifa that serves our game with commitment, transparency, and integrity."

Wenger is one of 18 Fifa officials named in a document preservation letter Uefa sent to Fifa threatening legal action.

Carlos Cordeiro - Infantino's senior adviser on global strategy and governance - is the only Fifa official to resign over the scandal, saying the proposal was "a bad deal for football" and would "mortgage football's future".

Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafstrom joined the criticism of the plan, writing in an internal memo to staff that the last week had been "difficult to comprehend and accept".

Grafstrom is seen as a close ally of Infantino, becoming Fifa's chief of staff after the Swiss was elected president in 2016. The Swede was evelated to secretary general, one of the most powerful positions in Fifa, in 2024.

"A sad and reproachable series of events - which were thankfully concluded with the project permanently abandoned - for as much as we feel dismayed by them, should not overshadow this reality," Grafstrom wrote.

"We have all been thrown into the middle of a turmoil, which is difficult to comprehend and accept.

"I urge you to remain focused on what has always united us: serving football and serving our 211 member associations, hand in hand with all relevant stakeholders and in full compliance with the Fifa statutes and Fifa regulations.

"I assure you that you as members of the administration, you will be defended and safeguarded from the political context we currently experience. You do not need to worry.

"Individuals, unstable moments and unfortunate episodes come and go. The institution, its mission and its responsibility towards world football continue, and that is why we should always keep our professionalism, sense of perspective and composure."

Fifa has been approached for comment.

title: Myanmar's detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi meets Red Cross official
description: Aug 3 () - Myanmar's detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi met with a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross on Monday, after years of questions over the health and well-bein...
fullText:
Aug 3 (Reuters) - Myanmar's detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi met with a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross on Monday, after years of questions over the health and well-being of the 81-year-old Nobel Peace Prize winner.

Suu Kyi has been in detention since February 2021, when an elected civilian government led ‌by her was ousted by Myanmar's military in a dawn coup, plunging the impoverished Southeast Asian nation into turmoil.

Since then, Suu Kyi's exact whereabouts and health condition have been ‌difficult to determine, with no foreign leader or envoy having publicly met with her despite requests for contact from countries in the region that have excluded Myanmar's leadership from their summits.

Suu Kyi met with Arnaud de Baecque, Resident Representative of ​the International Committee of the Red Cross to Myanmar, in the capital Naypyitaw on Monday, government spokesperson Khine Khine Soe said in a message via Telegram.

The ICRC confirmed that a delegate had met with Suu Kyi, without naming the official, while her son described the visit as the first positive development concerning his mother in more than five years.

In one of four photographs provided by the Myanmar government spokesperson, Suu Kyi is seen dressed in traditional Burmese attire and standing unaided, shaking hands with de Baecque.

In another, they are seated in a sparsely furnished, wood-panelled room containing only two chairs and a desk.

SON URGES CONTINUED ‌PRESSURE FOR SUU KYI'S RELEASE

The ICRC said the visit had met ⁠with its standards and procedures for visiting people deprived of liberty. "This included the opportunity to speak with Daw Aung San Suu Kyi in private," it said in a statement, using a Burmese honorific.

Suu Kyi's son, Kim Aris, told Reuters that the ICRC was not able to have a physician examine his mother ⁠but he said she seemed to be in good health and in good spirits.

"It's the first independent proof that I've had that she's actually alive for a long time now," he said in London. "So it's extremely meaningful."

Aris said that while he remained cautious, he hoped to be able to speak to his mother in time, and urged other governments to keep up the pressure on Myanmar to release her and other political prisoners.

Aris ​told ​Reuters in December that he had received only sporadic, second-hand details about his mother's heart, bone and gum problems - and ​had not heard from her in years.

The United Nations, whose special envoy on ‌Myanmar, Julie Bishop, has called repeatedly for independent, verifiable reports on Suu Kyi's circumstances, said it had taken note of the ICRC announcement and stressed the need for inclusive dialogue.

"We welcome this development and reiterate our call for the swift and unconditional release of all those arbitrarily detained, as a fundamental step towards conditions conducive to a credible and transparent political process," U.N. spokesperson Farhan Haq told a daily briefing in New York.

After a marathon run of secret trials following the 2021 coup, Suu Kyi, who was held under house arrest for a total of 15 years under a previous junta, was sentenced to 33 years' detention, convicted of charges ranging from corruption and inciting election fraud to violating state secrecy rules.

Her allies maintain that the charges were politically motivated and ‌aimed at sidelining the most popular politician in the country of 51 million people.

The sentence was later reduced, leaving ​her with 18 years still to serve, according to a member of her legal team.

Myanmar's military-backed administrations have repeatedly ​claimed that Suu Kyi, who is the daughter of Myanmar's independence hero General Aung San, ​is in "good health," even as international pressure has grown to allow independent verification.

After a meeting between Myanmar's foreign minister and counterparts from the regional ASEAN bloc ‌last month, Thailand's top diplomat Sihasak Phuangketkeow called for access to Suu Kyi.

ASEAN ​has barred Myanmar's leadership from its top meetings ​for failure to implement a peace roadmap.

In late April, following a military-engineered election that allowed former junta leader Min Aung Hlaing to become Myanmar's president, Suu Kyi was moved to house arrest.

In another of the photos provided by the Myanmar government offering a rare glimpse inside what appears to be her residence, Suu Kyi is seen cutting a birthday ​cake, with a clothes rack and storage boxes visible in the background.

A ‌fourth photograph is a close-up of the cake, inscribed with "Happy Birthday Aunty Suu 19.6.2026".

title: Van Gaal says he's open for a fourth coaching spell at Netherlands
description: Louis van Gaal said that he's open for a fourth coaching spell at the Netherlands national team. "I always want to help the Dutch Football Federation (KNVB), just as I also wanted to do at Ajax," Van Gaal told the Voetbal International in an interview published on Monday evening.
fullText:
Louis van Gaal said that he's open for a fourth coaching spell at the Netherlands national team.

"I always want to help the Dutch Football Federation (KNVB), just as I also wanted to do at Ajax," Van Gaal told the Voetbal International in an interview published on Monday evening.

"And with such a squad, there are of course possibilities. I also think that the Netherlands could still possibly become European or world champions, because 95% of the squad play abroad and often at good clubs."

Dutch media has suggested the 74-year-old as a potential successor to Ronald Koeman, who resigned following the Netherlands' early exit from the World Cup in North America last month.

Van Gaal said he's astonished with the fact that no ideal successor has been found so far and that coaches such as Arne Slot and Erik ten Hag have turned down the job.

"The only thing going on is that at this moment they still cannot get anyone and then my name comes up again. I find that rather unbelievable," he said.

"Four years ago at the World Cup in Qatar we lost on penalties in the quarter-finals and 'people' did not think our football was good enough. And those people now see me as the ideal man?"

He added that so far he hasn't had talks with the federation.

"I therefore have absolutely no idea what the KNVB wants," he said.

Van Gaal coached the national team in 2000-2001, 2012-2014 and 2021-2022. His best result was finishing in third at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil.

The KNVB will hope to find a new coach soon as their next game is on September 24 against Germany.

title: Itauma v Hrgovic upgraded to IBF world-title bout
description: British heavyweight Moses Itauma's fight against Filip Hrgovic on 29 August will be for the vacant IBF title.
fullText:
British heavyweight Moses Itauma's fight against Filip Hrgovic on 29 August will be for the vacant IBF title.

Itauma, 21, has been widely tipped as the next star of heavyweight boxing, with 12 knockouts in 14 professional victories.

Promoter Frank Warren told BBC Sport the IBF belt, vacated by Oleksandr Usyk in June, will be on the line at London's O2 Arena.

"A lot of people have high expectations of him as I have, by the way," Queensberry Promotions' Warren told BBC Sport.

"We signed him when he was 16. He was an amateur. We sponsored him and he turned professional with us. And he's been amazing and sort of taken the world by storm.

"This is a big moment for him. But I'm confident he can do it."

Itauma would become the youngest heavyweight champion since Mike Tyson if he beats Hrgovic.

He had initially been ordered to enter negotiations with Cuban Frank Sanchez for the vacant title and was given a deadline of 29 July.

However, Sanchez has agreed to step aside and will instead face the winner of the bout.

"We paid [Sanchez] some money. We said whoever wins the fight, you're not losing out and you'll get the opportunity to fight for the title against the winner," Warren added.

Itauma impressed in a fifth-round stoppage of American Jermaine Franklin in Manchester in March and stopped Briton Dillian Whyte in one round in August 2025.

Hrgovic, a 2016 Olympic bronze medallist, has won 20 professional fights. The 34-year-old stopped Briton Dave Allen in the third round in May.

"We know Hrgovic is going to come and give 100%, and 100% of him is hard work for anyone," Warren said.

Nigerian heritage key to my success - Itauma

Itauma handed everything on a plate - Hrgovic

A victory for Itauma could set up an all-British unification fight next year.

WBO champion Daniel Dubois defeated Fabio Wardley in May to become a two-time heavyweight world champion, and Warren confirmed the pair will contest a rematch in October.

Warren says should Itauma beat Hrgovic and then Sanchez, a fight against Ipswich's Wardley or Londoner Dubois for two world titles may take place at Wembley Stadium in 2027.

"It would be huge, absolutely huge. They're big punchers. These guys are big, big punchers. They're exciting. They're not in boring fights," Warren said.

Wardley and Itauma are both trained by Ben Davison, and Warren says the trainer will have to "make a decision" if the fight happens.

"I've seen best friends fight each other but they do it for the money they get, which pays the bills," Warren added.

Russian Murat Gassiev is the WBA champion, while Germany's Agit Kabayel holds the WBC title and is also signed to Queensberry.

Itauma could become the second-youngest British boxer in the modern era to win a professional world title. The Chatham fighter will be 21 years and 244 days old when the fight takes place.

Prince Naseem Hamed, at 21 years and 218 days, captured a world title at a younger age when he stopped Steve Robinson to win the WBO featherweight title in 1995.

Teddy Baldock won the vacant world bantamweight title against Archie Bell in 1927, aged 19 years and 346 days.

"Obviously I'm proud of what he's done up to now but if he does this I'll be the happiest guy around because he's such a nice guy," Warren said.

"He is a great advert for British boxing, world boxing and for sport."

title: Wall Street bulls are starting to admit the earnings bubble is real—and the 60/40 portfolio may be the first casualty
description: Goldman’s chief global equity strategist Peter Oppenheimer said, “There does not appear to be a valuation bubble, but there may be an earnings bubble.”
fullText:
For more than four decades, the investing world operated on a foundational assumption: that a portfolio consisting of 60% stocks and 40% bonds would protect you when markets turned. For roughly the past 20 years, a second assumption took hold alongside it: that a handful of dominant tech companies would keep growing into whatever price investors were willing to pay. This has taken on several shapes, with the FAANG companies morphing into the "Magnificent Seven" during the pandemic, and the AI boom crowning a new group of "hyperscalers."

But these assumptions are taking a hit from sources that rarely deliver bad news about the markets they cover.

Goldman Sachs, one of the Street's most consistently bullish research shops, published a note Monday authored by chief global equity strategist Peter Oppenheimer conceding that "there does not appear to be a valuation bubble, but there may be an earnings bubble" in the technology sector.

The same day, Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok wrote in his Daily Spark note that "the 60/40 portfolio is broken," arguing that with the AI trade slowing down and government debt projected to reach 175% of GDP, "neither the 60 nor the 40 responds to what made it work in the first place."

Both notes came after a week of Big Tech earnings that saw shockingly large moves both up and down for major tech firms, with analysts debating whether they reflected the true shape of the AI moat or "financial nihilism."

Microsoft made history with a 17% stock surge, adding nearly $500 billion in market capitalization in one day, its largest single-day move since the financial crisis year of 2008. In fact, Oppenheimer said Monday that the market is seeing things change in a way they haven't since the Great Recession.

The 60/40 rule wasn't always gospel. Its theoretical roots trace to Harry Markowitz's 1952 work on portfolio theory, but it only became institutional orthodoxy during the four-decade stretch of falling interest rates that began in the early 1980s. That decline let bonds do double duty as both income and ballast against equities, a dynamic that market analysts have called the "golden age" of investing.

Slok's warning isn't a reaction to one bad earnings season. He has argued since at least 2023 that rates would stay "higher for longer" than consensus expected. By late May 2026, he had sharpened that macro call into a specific yield-curve mechanism: Front-end rates were rising on sticky inflation; the middle of the curve was under pressure "because of hyperscaler issuance"; and long-end rates were climbing on "more Treasury supply and less Fed demand." His Aug. 3 argument that "the real risk emerges if the AI trade reverses or markets become more worried about government deficits" is a continuation of that multiyear thesis, not a new one.

title: Apple challenges UK government's latest demand for iCloud backdoor: report
description: Apple has appealed a new legal demand by the U.K. government, which critics say could threaten the privacy rights of users all over the world.
fullText:
Apple is challenging another legal demand by the U.K. government to access the encrypted data of its users in the country, according to the Financial Times.

The company reportedly filed a complaint with the U.K.’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal, a court that hears cases related to government surveillance, after the government last year issued a “technical capability notice”. The notice is a secret government legal order for demanding access to users’ data, even if the data is encrypted.

For critics, this kind of demand is the equivalent of requesting a backdoor into Apple’s cloud backups that have Advanced Data Protection (ADP) switched on, which makes the data end-to-end encrypted and inaccessible to anyone other than the customer, including to Apple.

This new challenge comes a year after a similar fight between Apple and the U.K. government. In early 2025, London issued a secret order to Apple demanding access to users’ encrypted iCloud backups, which was later dropped following the intervention of the Trump administration.

After the first order, the company reacted by removing the ability of U.K. users to use ADP. Then, in October, the U.K. issued a second order, which Apple is now challenging.

Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

title: Ireland 'laser-focused' on World Cup qualification
description: Ireland's five-game ODI series against Afghanistan this week marks the start of their preparations for next year's World Cup qualifying tournament.
fullText:
As he prepares to take charge of Ireland for the first time in a five-game ODI series against Afghanistan starting on Wednesday, new head coach Gary Wilson has challenged the side to make their own World Cup history.

Ireland have not qualified for the 50-over competition since 2015 but, as they return to the format for the first time in 15 months this week, Wilson says his squad are "laser-focused" on making it to South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia next autumn.

Wilson played in that tournament 11 years ago, and four years prior when the side famously toppled England in Bangalore (now Bengaluru), so knows well the impact such tournaments have in raising the side's profile at home and abroad.

"We're laser-focused on 50-over cricket right now for that reason," said Wilson of World Cup qualification.

"I've been lucky enough to be part of two and they are amazing experiences."

Stirling returns for Wilson's first Ireland ODIs

Security plans in place for any Afghanistan protests

Ireland are 12th in the ODI rankings and, as part of a keenly debated new format, will take part in a 10-team qualifier next year for just one guaranteed berth at the 2027 World Cup.

Another three teams will advance to a so-called Super Series directly preceding the tournament to decide the final spot in the 12-team field.

Despite the precarious path to even make it back to a World Cup, Wilson does not want his players to limit their ambition to just taking part.

"Irish cricket is really in its infancy in many ways and there's been a lot of firsts within the last 20 years," he said.

"We've had Ed Joyce as the first player to play for England, we've had the first World Cup in 2007, we've had the first Test win, why can't we go on and do something huge at a World Cup? If you'd said 30 or 40 years ago where the Irish rugby team would be now, you'd have got laughed at.

"Whether it's in our lifetime or not, one day we will do something amazing. A challenge I've put to this group is to create their own firsts. I think if we just stay focused, there's something big very close."

Should Ireland meet Wilson's ambitions, it will be in spite of a lack of 50-over cricket. In the three years since the 2023 edition of the World Cup, they have scheduled just 15 ODIs with three of those lost to the weather.

The series against Afghanistan - which Cricket Ireland CEO Sarah Keane has said comes with "moral discomfort" given the treatment of women in the Asian country - will be Ireland's first in the format since a 1-1 draw with West Indies in May 2025.

"It is a challenge of course, but it is what it is," said Wilson.

"We know it's a barrier but there's not any point in talking about it, we can't change it. We have played other cricket within that period.

"Would I have wanted more? Of course, I'd have wanted loads, but that's not to be. We've got what we've got and we get on with it and attempt to beat Afghanistan in this series."

Ireland at least come in with recent white-ball form after June's historic T20 series win over India.

The 2-0 victory at Stormont, Ireland's first wins over the T20 world champions in any format, made global headlines but Wilson is keen to draw a line under the feat.

"More than anything those results probably made people stand up and think and it's something we can try and work off the back of as a wider organisation," he said.

"In terms of the team, we mustn't get carried away with two results. You wouldn't change them for the world, they were phenomenal, but they're in the past now. We must start again against Afghanistan."

Bowler Jai Moondra, the breakout star of the India series, will make his 50-over debut against Afghanistan, while Paul Stirling, who retains the ODI captaincy despite relinquishing the T20 role, seamer Mark Adair and all-rounder Curtis Campher all return to the panel.

Against a side who have travelled with the likes of Rashid Kahn and Ibrahim Zadran in their touring squad, Ireland will however be without Josh Little, Craig Young, Barry McCarthy, Matt Hollard and Jordan Neil through injury.

The wins over India were the final games under previous head coach Heinrich Malan who was replaced by his former assistant Wilson less than 24 hours after the series concluded in what Cricket Ireland called a "planned transition".

While Wilson said the role is one he had his "eye on" since retiring in 2020, he acknowledges it will come with a different set of responsibilities to those he had under Malan.

"Obviously the relationships will have to change slightly because you become the person responsible for picking players and not picking players," he said.

"By default, some players aren't going to be happy and previously those players maybe would have turned to you.

"That's a different dynamic, but I base my whole coaching philosophy around communication and I think if you can remain pretty steady with that, while difficult conversations are hard, at least if you're honest, players know what to expect from you."

title: USA cricketer gets eight-year ban for match-fixing
description: United States international Bodugum Akhilesh Reddy is banned from all forms of cricket for eight years after being found guilty of match-fixing.
fullText:
United States international Bodugum Akhilesh Reddy has been banned from all forms of cricket for eight years after being found guilty of match-fixing.

An International Cricket Council (ICC) Anti-Corruption Tribunal found Reddy breached three counts of the sport's anti-corruption code during the Abu Dhabi T10 League in the United Arab Emirates last year.

The 26-year-old was part of the Aspin Stallions side that also featured former India off-spinner Harbhajan Singh and England's Sam Billings and which reached the Abu Dhabi T10 final in 2025.

The spinner made his USA debut against Cayman Islands in April 2025 and has played four T20s for the country.

The ICC said the tribunal found Reddy guilty of "attempting to fix, contrive or otherwise influence improperly, or being party to an agreement or effort to fix or contrive in any way or otherwise influence improperly, the result, progress, conduct or other aspect of matches in the ADT10 2025".

He was also found guilty of encouraging another participant to engage in match-fixing and obstructing the investigation "through deletion of data and messages from a mobile device".

The ban has been backdated to 21 November 2025 when Reddy was provisionally suspended after making two appearances in the T10 League.

title: Vinicius’ Real Madrid current contract details as renewal talks deadlocked due to image rights
description: Vinicius Jr.’s contract situation remains one of Real Madrid’s biggest unresolved issues, with negotiations stretching back to the aftermath of the 2025 Club World Cup, shortly after Xabi Alonso t...
fullText:
Vinicius Jr.’s contract situation remains one of Real Madrid’s biggest unresolved issues, with negotiations stretching back to the aftermath of the 2025 Club World Cup, shortly after Xabi Alonso took charge.

Indeed, as reported by AS, it was during that period that the player’s representatives held their last face-to-face meeting with the club, when an agreement appeared close before talks unexpectedly stalled.

Negotiations are now set to resume from that point.

During that meeting at Valdebebas, Vinicius reportedly made a significant concession on his original salary demands, which had initially been close to €30 million net per season.

Real Madrid also improved their offer, bringing both sides much closer together. Despite the progress, the renewal was never finalized.

Neither party was willing to make the final compromise, leaving an agreement that seemed imminent unsigned.

Still no agreement over renewal. (Photo by Lars Baron/Getty Images)

Vinicius is now seeking a salary of around €20 million net per season, an increase of roughly €5 million over his current earnings.

His existing contract, signed in 2022 and officially announced in October 2023, runs until 2027 and is worth €75 million net over five seasons, averaging €15 million per year.

The agreement was structured progressively. He began on approximately €10 million net per season. His salary rose annually to reach around €18 million in the final year.

The 26-year-old Brazilian also received an additional €2 million per season after winning FIFA’s The Best award, a bonus that would also have been triggered by winning the Ballon d’Or.

While salary remains important, image rights have become one of the biggest sticking points in negotiations.

Kylian Mbappe controls almost 100% of his image rights, a structure that helps facilitate his overall financial package at Real Madrid.

Vinicius is now looking for a similar arrangement. As one of football’s biggest commercial stars, the Brazilian has endorsement deals with 18 international brands.

These include Nike, Apple, PlayStation, Pepsi, Gatorade, Boss, Visa, Marriott Bonvoy, Havaianas, UNESCO, Clear, Rexona, Omo, Vivo, Prada, Dubai Tourism, and Betnacional.

The winger is also believed to be interested in receiving a renewal bonus, similar in concept to the signing bonus Mbappe received when joining Real Madrid.

Vinicius’ current deal expires in 2027, meaning that from January he would be permitted to negotiate freely with clubs outside Spain if no renewal is agreed.

As such, Real Madrid are seeking a quick resolution, one way or the other.

The latest information from the Brazilian’s camp suggests his priority remains staying at Real Madrid by signing a new contract.

Having returned to Valdebebas today after his vacation, Vinicius is expected to hold a decisive meeting with Jose Mourinho and Real Madrid’s senior leadership in the coming hours to discuss his future.

title: Chevron CEO warns Iran conflict has created 'very real' threat to global oil supplies as gas prices climb
description: Chevron CEO Mike Wirth warns of "very real" risks to oil supply as the Strait of Hormuz, Red Sea and Black Sea face growing threats amid Iran conflict.
fullText:
Chevron CEO Mike Wirth warned of "very real" dangers for the global oil industry as tensions escalate in Iran and Houthi attacks on Saudi oil facilities fuel concerns over a potential new shipping crisis.

His comments come as oil prices climb following President Donald Trump's pause on U.S. strikes against Iran and as Saudi Arabia reportedly builds an international coalition to protect vital shipping routes.

"We now see, not only the Strait of Hormuz, but the Red Sea and the Black Sea have risks and uncertainties. So, some of the challenges have expanded, and the risks to supply are very real," Wirth said during an appearance on "Sunday Morning Futures."

Trump Warns Iran Fighting Isn't Over As He Vows Us Will 'Win' As Talks Fade

While oil demand remains strong around the world, Wirth said energy markets are "fragile and uncertain" as the U.S. conflict with Iran festers into a sixth month and as global inventories continue to decline.

"The world energy system has been stressed and the need for supplies to markets and customers has never been higher," the Chevron CEO said.

The Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most vital trade routes, is one of the most contentious aspects of the United States conflict with Iran. Traffic has sunk to only a handful of vessels passing through the waterway each day.

Recent Houthi attacks on another vital Middle East shipping route, the Red Sea, have raised fresh concerns about the reliability of that corridor.

Steve Forbes Urges Trump To Keep The Strait Of Hormuz Open At All Costs

"I think the unfortunate thing is that energy assets have been targeted in this conflict. And what that means is it degrades the capacity of the energy system to meet global demand," Wirth said. "And how quickly that comes back will be one of the things that determines when markets actually get back to some sort of a new equilibrium."

"We've seen supply constrained, we've seen damage to infrastructure. And we have new risks that I think will be priced into the market on shipping."

U.S. crude oil is trading at roughly $84 per barrel, while the national average price for a gallon of gasoline stands at $4.09 – nearly $1 higher than the $3.15 average one year ago, according to AAA.

Despite the growing geopolitical uncertainty, Chevron's production is up 20% year-on-year, with a 5% increase from Q1 to Q2 of 2026. The oil giant also set a record for producing more than 2 million barrels of oil equivalent in one day, an all-time high for the U.S., Wirth said.

title: UFC or PFL? Nurmagomedov to decide future 'very soon'
description: PFL lightweight world champion Usman Nurmagomedov will decide on his future "very soon" after becoming a free agent, according to his cousin and coach Khabib Nurmagomedov.
fullText:
PFL lightweight world champion Usman Nurmagomedov will decide on his future "very soon" after becoming a free agent, according to his cousin and coach Khabib Nurmagomedov.

Russia's Nurmagomedov knocked out American Archie Colgan in New York last week to retain his title in the final fight on his contract with the PFL.

The 28-year-old, who is undefeated with 22 victories, is widely-considered one of the biggest talents outside the UFC and has long been touted to eventually sign with the promotion.

But the end of his contract comes amid an exciting new chapter for the PFL after the organisation merged with Most Valuable Promotions (MVP) last week.

In a statement on Instagram, Khabib praised Nurmagomedov and compared him to team-mate and UFC welterweight champion Islam Makhachev, before revealing negotiations around his next move will take place "over the next month".

"Usman has shown and proven over the last couple of years that he is the best lightweight outside the UFC. Not with words, but with his performances," said Khabib.

"When I said in 2020 that Islam was the best at that time, there were many people who disagreed. Believe me guys, there are levels to this game.

"You will see for yourselves what happens next. There will be negotiations over the next month, and very soon you will find out for yourselves which league he will continue competing in."

Nurmagomedov's first-round knockout of Colgan was the second defence of his PFL belt and sixth in total after the Bellator title was rebranded in 2025.

After the bout, Nurmagomedov asked MVP co-owner Jake Paul for a "bonus", to which the American replied, "next fight if you get a knockout, I'll buy you a car".

Nurmagomedov raised questions about his future in the organisation by responding, "brother let's talk about today - we don't know what's going to happen tomorrow".

Following the UFC's event in Belgrade on Saturday, the promotion's president Dana White replied "sure" while sporting a wry smile when he was asked about the prospect of signing Nurmagomedov.

Paul has been a frequent critic of White and UFC fighter pay, and Nurmagomedov made reference to that in the closing words of his post-fight interview.

"MVP, they always trash talk about Dana saying he doesn't pay - now we're gonna see how they're gonna pay," said Nurmagomedov.

Fans have long wondered how Nurmagomedov would fare in the UFC with his career following a similar trajectory to cousin and coach, Khabib.

Former UFC lightweight champion Khabib retired undefeated in 2020 having won all 29 professional fights and cementing his legacy as one of the sport's greatest-ever fighters.

Khabib's game was built on relentless pressure and wrestling and although Nurmagomedov is fine grappler, he differs from his legendary cousin by controlling fights with an array of eye-catching kicks.

Like Khabib, Nurmagomedov is undefeated, but apart from two gruelling bouts with Paul Hughes in 2025, he has rarely been tested to his limit in the PFL.

Signing with the UFC would open doors to a number of mouth-watering fights, and although the move would be beneficial for his brand and name, financially the prospect is not as clear.

The UFC gives about 20% of revenue to fighter pay - a policy which has been criticised by fighters - while it remains to be seen what pay structure the PFL and MVP's merger will implement.

Whichever promotion pays Nurmagomedov the most may influence his decision, with the Russian admitting he values money over legacy in interviews following his win over Colgan.

title: Emma Finucane: Can cycling's new star be beaten?
description: Experts explain what sets apart this "generational talent" who is already an Olympic, world and commonwealth champion at just 23.
fullText:
Emma Finucane left Glasgow with four Commonwealth gold medals. She had become the conversation inside the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome.

Not simply because she kept winning but because of the way she was winning.

A dominant week in Glasgow does not automatically make someone the best rider on the planet.

The world's best track cyclists are spread well beyond the Commonwealth.

As the week unfolded, conversations drifted away from the medal table.

And where this "generational talent" might be by the time the Los Angeles Olympics arrive in 2028.

BBC Sport spoke to the people who worked closest with Finucane throughout the Games to understand why those inside the velodrome believed they had witnessed far more than just an outstanding medal haul.

Those people do not first talk about Finucane's power or speed, but rather her methodical preparation.

"She's a dream to coach. It's the fact that she gets everything right off the bike in the lead-up to it is why she's able to perform on the track," said Team Wales sprint coach Rachel Draper.

Rob Partridge, a former professional cyclist who was part of Team Wales' coaching staff in Glasgow, describes an athlete who takes complete ownership of every detail.

"Everything she does is elite. She'll map everything out, be clear and concise and be first to send it," Partridge explains.

"Everything is super crisp and planned out."

Finucane's record-breaking day to remember

'I can't believe I'm living this life' - Finucane

'A huge success' - Wales win 31 medals at Glasgow Games

Preparation explained part of the conversation. Watching her ride explained the rest.

Again and again, people used the same word. Smooth.

"She's got a beautiful style. You could put a teacup on her back and it would not spill," said two-time Commonwealth champion Katherine Bates.

"She's got an exceptionally strong core. She does not move at all on the bike, even when putting out maximum power."

Paralympic gold medalist and Finucane's former Great Britain team-mate, Jenny Holl, believes that style is difficult to teach.

"Emma looks like she's one with the bike," she reveres.

"She's so smooth, so dialed. She never looks like she's fighting with it and, for me, that's the biggest difference. That fluidity seems to give her that extra gear."

Finucane's positioning has taken years of refining and discipline.

"She's so low but that's really hard work. She's trained herself to be in that position," explained Partridge.

"The work she's put in, the focus on the position and the discipline on her line, all these things add up to making her what she is."

Perhaps the best example came in the women's 1km time trial.

While most of the field opted for specialist time-trial handlebars, Finucane chose conventional drop handlebars.

Finucane left Paris an Olympic champion after winning gold in the team sprint.

But Holl believes those 2024 Games left her wanting more.

"The bronze medals in the [individual] sprint and keirin in Paris, where she wanted gold, have given Emma that extra boost of motivation," she said.

"She was a brilliant athlete in Paris, but now we really are seeing something special."

Another quality kept surfacing throughout the week - composure.

Bates says Finucane rarely betrays what she is feeling.

"She's so determined, but she's also so calm. Even under pressure, you just never see anything on her face but composure," she said.

"She barely even cracks a smile until it's over. That's part of how she prepares for an event.

"It's a big build-up. She maintains that and when it's over, she releases the pressure valve and moves on to the next one."

For Draper, these Games in the red lycra of Wales mattered deeply to Finucane.

"Emma put a lot of pressure on herself to perform at these Games," she said.

"She's already world champion, Olympic champion, but for Emma, this has meant everything.

"Seeing that emotion for her on the podium has just been really special for us as a team."

When Bates reflects on the greatest female sprinters she has watched, her thoughts turn to Anna Meares, Victoria Pendleton and Kristina Vogel.

"Emma Finucane is like a combination of them all rolled up into one neat package," explained the former world points race champion.

"Some have incredible acceleration, others are very good at the back end of a long race.

"There are others whose skills are just superior. She's got excellent skills, acceleration and really good staying power, so it makes her a triple threat.

"She's young that she hasn't gone to four Olympic Games yet, or 15 World Championships that some of the others have.

"But I'm fairly confident in a decade's time we'll be looking back at her career, just wondrous of what she's been able to achieve."

Then comes the line that echoed around the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome.

"A lot of the countries are looking at her and thinking, 'Is it even worth trying to beat her? Or are we going there for a silver medal?'," admitted Australian Bates.

"That's a big statement two years out [from the Olympics] but that's the kind of talent we're looking at."

Four gold medals made Finucane the most successful cyclist of the Games and her nation's most decorated female Commonwealth Games athlete.

For those who know the sport best, they may also have been a glimpse of what comes next.

title: Newcastle Makes Official Announcement Before Matthias Jaissle Hiring

fullText:
Newcastle United’s search for a new first-choice goalkeeper is finally over after months of speculation surrounding the position and a lengthy list of reported targets throughout the summer.

The Magpies officially announced the signing of Czech Republic international Lukas Hornicek from Braga on Monday, with the 24-year-old arriving on a five-year contract after Newcastle activated his €30 million (£25.7 million) release clause.

The Athletic reported the deal’s figures, revealing it would be worth the full value of the goalkeeper’s release clause, which Newcastle activated over the weekend.

Hornicek becomes Newcastle’s fifth first-team signing of the summer following the arrivals of Ewen Jaouen, Bazoumana Toure, Sean Steur and Aladji Bamba. The goalie has already joined the team at Newcastle’s preseason training camp in Spain, with new manager Matthias Jaissle in town but still not officially hired, as no word from the club has emerged since Eddie Howe’s exit.

Speaking after completing the move, Hornicek described the transfer as a major opportunity.

“The last few days have been an emotional rollercoaster from when I first heard about the move and now I’m so happy to be here,” Hornicek said. “It’s a brilliant opportunity in a new league, which I’m very excited about.”

The goalkeeper also highlighted Newcastle’s supporters as one of the attractions behind the move.

“I know Newcastle is a huge football city, with 52,000 fans at St. James’ Park creating an incredible atmosphere and pushing the team every game,” Hornicek said. “I can’t wait to play in front of them.”

Sporting director Ross Wilson believes the club has secured one of Europe’s brightest young goalkeepers.

“His progress in recent years has been remarkable and he has firmly established himself as one of Europe’s top young goalkeepers,” Wilson said. “We knew there would be no shortage of clubs interested in acquiring Lukáš this summer after everything he achieved last season, but it quickly became evident how keen he was to be a part of what we are building here.”

Hornicek played a key role in Braga’s run to the Europa League semifinals last season, helping the Portuguese side finish fourth in Portugal’s Primeira Liga while keeping 12 clean sheets and conceding just 33 league goals. He also earned his first senior Czech Republic cap earlier this year before being included in the nation’s World Cup squad.

title: When the Future Doesn't Need Us
description: What does the world look like when AI outcompetes humans?
fullText:
Today, the world is made of people. This gives people a tiny measure of
leverage: factory workers can sabotage the machines and halt production, truck
drivers can strike and halt the entire economy, the police can stand back and
let a protest topple the government, the military can
mutiny. This sets a limit to how much the powerful can abuse the
powerless: no matter how powerful someone is, how much money they have, how many
divisions they command, they are still embedded in a society. They need other
people to survive, and to maintain their quality of life. And those people can,
essentially, veto the political order by withdrawing their contribution to it.

AI changes this. If AI works the factories, drives the trucks, does most of the
white collar work, fights the wars, then humans become materially powerless. We
lose one type of leverage against power. We become disempowered. When
people talk about AI taking jobs, the main problems they worry about are poverty
and meaning, but I think more people should be worried about disempowerment.

But what if there is no mass unemployment? After all, we’ve spent two hundred
years automating one job after another, and every advanced economy is de facto
at full employment. We keep discovering new, higher-level, better-paying jobs to
do. So maybe the AIs take today’s jobs, and humans move one level up, to work
newer jobs. Alex Imas, in What will be scarce?, describes
what this looks like:

As commodity production gets automated, income and employment flow toward the
sectors with high income elasticity: what I am calling the relational sector,
including the arts but also care, education, hospitality, therapy, personal
services, craftsmanship, and community, where the human element is part of the
value.

If the model is right, the durable jobs of the future won’t be about
monitoring AI systems or prompt engineering. Those are transitional roles in
the automated sector. The durable jobs will be in the relational sector, where
the human element is the product itself.

Some already exist and are growing: nurses, therapists, teachers, boutique
fitness instructors, personal chefs, bespoke tailors, craft brewers, live
performers, spiritual guides, childcare workers, and many varieties of
hospitality and care work. Others are emerging: experience designers, human-AI
collaboration artists, provenance certifiers, community curators. Many haven’t
been invented yet, just as six out of ten jobs people hold today didn’t exist
in 1940.

So, in this world, we get mass job displacement, but not mass unemployment. I
argue that in this world, we’d still be disempowered.

If all the podcasters in the world go on strike, what happens? Nothing. Same for
the boutique fitness instructors, personal chefs, craft brewers, etc. The
problem with the “relational economy” is that while these jobs are generally
nicer than working in manufacturing, and might pay better, they put you further
away from material reality. A worker at an assembly line can sabotage the
machines; whereas an executive sitting in an office on the other side of the
country, what material power do they have? It’s not like the factories are all
rigged to blow, as a “pull lever in case of nationalization” contingency. I
doubt even Elon would do that.

In a sense it’s the dual version of being a medieval peasant. Peasants had a lot
of material leverage—they grew all the food—but were illiterate and poor and
dispersed, so they could not coordinate to exploit that leverage. People in
industrial societies are literate, relatively wealthy, and concentrated in urban
centers: they have material leverage and the ability to exploit it. People in
post-AI societies will be in constant communication, they may be literate and
educated, but they will have no material power whatever. And so they will have
no way to physically withdraw the consent of the governed.

In the post-AGI world, people have no way to withdraw the consent of the
governed. They can’t resist economically, because they are economically
unnecessary: if they still have jobs, they won’t be materially vital jobs. Even
if they could resist, they can’t coordinate their resistance, because AGI will
make mass surveillance (the physical and legal infrastructure for which already
exists) a thousandfold more effective, since with intelligence too cheap to
meter, you can have a superhumanly-capable intelligence analyst assigned to each
human. And if the AIs fight the wars, they can also fight the civil wars. So
people can’t resist violently either, because drones controlled by powerful AGI
almost certainly have a better K/D ratio than humans with rifles (and are
cheaper to build).

Who has power in this world? The few humans who give orders to the powerful AIs
that control the killing machines. And probably not for long, since sooner or
later those humans will be usurped by their AIs.

It might be the case that liberal democracies can remain liberal and democratic
despite not needing their voters. But that sounds like a fragile arrangement, in
which liberal democracy is a spandrel, which exists more because of
inertia than because it’s necessary.

If we get powerful AGI, but none of this happens: why didn’t it happen? Some
possibilities, sorted by decreasing likelihood:

If you’re already convinced, you can stop reading. But, see, after writing the
first version of this post, I wasn’t convinced. Humans and Claudes made a number
of counterarguments that I felt were important. Am I fooling myself? So I sat
down to think some more. What does it mean for “people” to be “empowered”? What
does “disempowerment” mean? Does it mean anything rigorous, or is it just an
emotional cue?

Let’s say a group of people is empowered if they have a say in the political
order of the state they live in. Voters in a democratic society are empowered,
at least in the aggregate, while serfs in the Russian Empire were disempowered.

Who is empowered, in general? Historically, in many places: people with weapons,
asabiyyah, and the ability to coordinate their actions. So, maybe we
can say that power equals violence plus coordination.

(What about priests and other such groups who have power despite not fighting or
working? Listen, we can’t be here all day. This isn’t meant to be a complete
theory of political science and I’ve already gone too deep with the LaTeX and
the logical notation.)

Now, voters in modern democracies have a say in the political order, though they
are not part of a military elite. Why? They have coordination (thanks to mass
literacy and modern communications) but they generally don’t threaten
paramilitary violence. What do they have that can substitute for violence? Maybe
it’s that people do all the work, and if they stop doing their jobs, the army
runs out of food, police don’t get paid, etc., and unlike medieval peasants,
modern people can coordinate. So maybe we can refine the formula to:

In other words, for a group to be empowered, they need:

What about the Soviet Union? They had high rates of literacy, and relatively
modern communication technology: why didn’t the people exploit their economic
leverage against the state to gain political rights? “Because the state would
kill them” is not a good enough explanation because it proves too much: under
that model, no country would liberalize and democratize. I think a reasonable
explanation is that the state’s repression was enough to effectively neuter
people’s ability to coordinate: every communication technology was surveilled
and censored.

Now, doesn’t this argument imply that, as a country’s employment moves towards
services, the country’s politics should become more authoritarian, while in
reality we observe the opposite? But whether a country’s economy is 5% or 95%
services, the material side of the economy is equally vital. So “aggregate
empowerment” remains as employment becomes more and more abstract. Consider
France, where the economy is ~80% services, but the last 20% can still paralyze
the country through strikes. In a sense every knowledge worker is free-riding on
the ability of truck drivers and dock workers to shut down the economy. I don’t
greatly like this counter-counterargument, though, because it’s hard to falsify:
it implies that countries might remain liberal democracies until AGI replaces
all humans in material work, at which point the state can go “that’s what we
wanted you to think!” and go full authoritarian.
